purpose: Digoxin is used to treat certain heart conditions, including heart failure and a type of irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. It helps your heart beat more regularly and with more strength. This can reduce symptoms like shortness of breath and swelling in your legs.
how_it_works: Digoxin works by slowing down the electrical signals in your heart so it beats in a more controlled, steady rhythm. It also helps the heart muscle squeeze more powerfully with each beat, so your heart pumps blood more efficiently. Think of it as giving your heart a more organized and stronger pumping action.
common_side_effects: Some people feel nauseated, lose their appetite, or have an upset stomach. You might experience dizziness, headache, or feel unusually tired. Some people notice blurred vision or see yellow-green halos around lights, which is important to report to your doctor right away.
warnings: Digoxin has a very narrow safe range in your blood, meaning too little won't help and too much can be dangerous. Never take more than prescribed, and do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor right away if you have a slow or irregular heartbeat, confusion, vision changes, or severe nausea and vomiting. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure the level in your body is safe. Many medicines and even some foods can interact with digoxin, so always check before starting anything new.
typical_dosing: Most adults take between 0.125 mg and 0.25 mg once a day by mouth. Your doctor will find the right dose for you based on your age, weight, kidney function, and blood tests. Always take it at the same time each day, and never skip or double up on doses.
